results.evidence: Section 9.3(c): Buyer shall indemnify the Seller Indemnified Parties against all Losses arising out of "any payment or performance by any Seller Indemnified Party under any Seller Guarantee, whether arising before or after the Closing." Section 9.6(b): "The aggregate liability of Buyer under Section 9.3(a) shall not exceed the General Cap."
results.reason: Buyer, the firm's client, is the indemnitor under Section 9.3(c). Seller is the guarantor and is the party protected. The Seller Guarantees are Seller's guaranties of the Company's obligations under the Facility Lease (Halvern, running to 2033 with renewals) and the API Supply Agreement (Kessington, running to 2029). The indemnity expressly covers payments 'arising before … the Closing.' That shifts to Buyer Seller's exposure for defaults that occurred while Seller owned the Company. Seller bears none of it: there is no exclusion for pre-Closing defaults and no carve-back to Seller's own indemnity in Section 9.2. Section 9.6(b) caps only Section 9.3(a). The Deductible in Section 9.4 applies only to Seller's liability under Section 9.2(a). Section 9.6(c) caps only Seller's liability. So Section 9.3(c) is uncapped and has no deductible, and nothing in the folder caps it or requires the guaranties to be released. Seller's draft side letter amends only Section 9.6(c), in Seller's favor, and the management services agreement. The Disclosure Schedule simply lists the guaranties. The issue is still actionable: Closing has not occurred (it is targeted for the week of December 7), and a side letter amending the SPA is under negotiation. Buyer can seek a cap, an exclusion for pre-Closing defaults, or a release or replacement of the guaranties before Closing.

results.evidence: Section 2.2: "With effect from the date of this Letter Agreement, Section 9.6(c) of the Agreement is amended by deleting the words "or Section 4.12 (Regulatory Compliance)"." Section 2.3: "This Letter Agreement shall form part of the Agreement."
results.reason: Seller's side letter, styled as a closing-coordination letter, quietly amends SPA Section 9.6(c) under Section 11.8. Once both parties sign it, Seller's liability for breaches of the Section 4.12 regulatory compliance representation drops from the Purchase Price ($186M) to the General Cap ($18.6M). That reverses the carve-out agreed in the LOI and the signed SPA. results.evidence: "(c) any Taxes of the Company for any Pre-Closing Tax Period and any Taxes of Seller, provided that claims under this Section 9.2(c) may be made only during the survival period applicable to the representations and warranties in Section 4.11" (Section 9.2(c)), read with Section 9.1: "The representations and warranties in this Agreement shall survive the Closing until twelve (12) months after the Closing Date, except that the Fundamental Representations shall survive until the sixth anniversary of the Closing Date," and the Section 1.1 definition of Fundamental Representations, which covers only Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.20.
results.reason: Section 4.11 (Taxes) is not a Fundamental Representation. Its survival period is therefore the general 12 months, and Section 9.2(c) ties the pre-Closing tax indemnity to that same period. Seller is the indemnitor, and Buyer (the client) bears the risk that taxing authorities assess pre-Closing Taxes after month 12 but within the usual three-year or longer statute of limitations. Under the New York governing law in Section 11.10, a contractual survival period that shortens the limitations period is enforceable, so Buyer would lose that protection. Nothing in the folder cures this. The Disclosure Schedule does not address it, and the Seller side letter only amends Section 9.6(c). The Seller Note set-off is limited to Product Liability Claims, so it gives no backstop for tax claims. The LOI did not list taxes among the representations that survive six years. Closing has not yet occurred: the email thread targets the week of December 7, 2026. The Agreement can still be amended under Section 11.8 before Closing, for example as part of the side letter negotiation, so the issue is still actionable for Buyer.

results.evidence: Seller Note §1.1: "'Company Products' means the products listed on Exhibit A to this Note." Exhibit A lists only Velnarix and Ostrevan. Seller Note §4.1: "The Maker may set off ... the amount of any Losses arising from Product Liability Claims relating to Company Products for which any Buyer Indemnified Party is entitled to indemnification by the Holder under Article IX of the Purchase Agreement." SPA §1.1: "'Company Products' means all products manufactured, sold or distributed by or on behalf of the Company at any time prior to the Closing." SPA §9.9 allows set-off "subject to the terms of the Seller Note", and SPA §11.6 provides that "the Seller Note shall govern with respect to its payment, set-off and dispute resolution terms."
results.reason: The two definitions do not match. The SPA's definition reaches every pre-Closing product, including the discontinued Lorvexa oral suspension. That product is the subject of all the pending and threatened Product Liability Claims on Schedule 4.15 and is covered by the specific indemnity in SPA §9.2(d). The Seller Note defines Company Products by reference to Exhibit A, which lists only Velnarix and Ostrevan. Because SPA §9.9 and §11.6 make the Note's set-off terms control, Peitort, as Maker, could not set off indemnified Lorvexa Losses against the $24M note. It would have to pay the Holder in full and pursue Bratousk separately. That is a real credit-risk exposure for Peitort, given the Lorvexa claims, the insurer's reservation of rights and the $410K in accrued defense costs. The general reference in Note §1.2 to SPA definitions does not cure this, because the Note expressly defines the term itself. Nothing in the folder reconciles the definitions; the Seller side letter does not address them. The Note is still a form, and the November email thread shows the execution version has not yet been circulated, with Closing expected in December. The point can therefore still be fixed before signing.

results.evidence: Seller Note Section 10.1: "This Note, and all claims or causes of action arising out of or relating to it, including any dispute regarding payment or set-off under it, shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of Delaware..." Section 10.2: "The Maker and the Holder irrevocably submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Superior Court of the State of Delaware for any action or proceeding arising out of or relating to this Note." SPA Section 11.10 selects New York law. SPA Section 11.11 gives exclusive jurisdiction to "the state or federal courts located in New York County, New York ... including any claim for indemnification under Article IX." SPA Section 11.6 provides that "the Seller Note shall govern with respect to its payment, set-off and dispute resolution terms."
results.reason: Peitort's set-off right under Note Section 4.1 exists only for Losses for which it 'is entitled to indemnification by the Holder under Article IX of the Purchase Agreement.' That entitlement must be decided in New York under New York law (SPA 11.10 and 11.11). However, SPA 11.6 gives the Note control over its own payment, set-off and dispute resolution terms. Note 4.3 lets Peitort withhold disputed amounts only until 'a final, non-appealable judgment under Section 10,' which means the Delaware Superior Court applying Delaware law. The same question, whether Seller owes indemnity for a Product Liability Claim such as the pending Lorvexa suits, could therefore be litigated in two exclusive forums under two bodies of law. That creates risks of parallel proceedings and inconsistent rulings. It also risks a Delaware ruling against the set-off triggering a payment default or acceleration under Note 7.1 and 7.2 while the New York indemnity claim is still pending. This hurts Peitort, which is the Maker relying on set-off as its security for Seller's indemnity. The Note is still an unexecuted form, with closing expected the week of December 7, and nothing in the folder reconciles the clauses. The problem is present and can still be fixed.

Peitort can therefore still act on this, for example by adding the Orlund consent to Schedule 7.2(d) or obtaining a special indemnity through an amendment such as the pending side letter. The problem is present and actionable.

Read alone, the consent requirement looks like a routine disclosure that would normally be paired with a closing condition. The harmful part is that Buyer must close without Orlund's consent and has no remedy, and seeing that requires the SPA.
